units.title: Trajectory objectives and the likelihood-ratio identity
outcomes: Factor a trajectory likelihood and identify which factors depend on policy parameters.
Derive the score-function estimator from expected return, with its support and differentiation assumptions.
Check the estimator against an exactly enumerated policy objective.
units.why: The environment need not be differentiable to optimize a stochastic policy. This identity supplies the gradient used by REINFORCE and later language-policy updates.

next.note: Turn the trajectory estimator into an implementable update.

study.title: CS 185/285 Lecture 5: Policy Gradients
study.locator: Slides 3 to 7: objective, trajectory factorization, direct differentiation and the sampled gradient

study.title: Part 3: Intro to Policy Optimization
study.locator: Deriving the Simplest Policy Gradient, facts 1 to 5 and Derivation for Basic Policy Gradient
study.depth: Stop before Implementing the Simplest Policy Gradient.

focus: Use the trajectory contract from Trajectories, episodes, horizons, discounting, termination and truncation. Include the initial-state law, each policy factor and each transition factor.

For a fixed environment and parameter-independent reward, only policy factors contribute to the trajectory score. Differentiability, fixed support and a valid interchange of derivative and expectation are assumptions, not consequences of sampling.
The score has mean zero: \(\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)]=0\). Multiplying it by return creates the learning signal.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(\nabla_\theta J=\mathbb{E}[R(\tau)\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)]\). Check a one-step Bernoulli policy with \(p=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\theta)=1/4\), reward 2 for action 1 and -1 for action 0: \(J=3p-1=-1/4\) and \(dJ/d\theta=3p(1-p)=9/16\). Enumerate both actions and recover the same gradient from their scores.
traps: Differentiating a sampled reward as if the sampled action were a differentiable path through the environment. The score-function estimator differentiates the sampling law instead.
Dropping a reward or transition derivative when those functions actually share policy parameters. The displayed estimator assumes they do not.
Summing action probabilities rather than log probabilities along a trajectory. Independent conditional factors multiply; their logs add.

selfTest.q: Why can an unknown transition model disappear from the score?
selfTest.a: Its log derivative is zero when the transition law has no policy parameters. Its effect remains in the sampled state distribution and rewards.

selfTest.q: What changes if the return explicitly depends on policy parameters?
selfTest.a: Add \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta R_\theta(\tau)]\) to the likelihood-ratio term, under the same differentiation assumptions.

selfTest.q: Does an action-dependent reward require a differentiable reward function?
selfTest.a: No. Dependence on a sampled action is already handled by the trajectory likelihood. Explicit dependence on policy parameters is a separate issue.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the policylab exact-enumeration policy-gradient oracle.
units.stopWhen: You derive the trajectory score without notes and match the one-step gradient by direct differentiation and exact enumeration.

fit.verdict: The lecture and Spinning Up supply the full derivation; the mini-project supplies an independent gradient oracle.

units.title: The policy-gradient theorem and REINFORCE
outcomes: Derive the policy-gradient theorem using state visitation and conditional action values.
Implement a REINFORCE update with explicit discounting, trajectory reduction and detached return weights.
Match the expected update to exact enumeration and a finite difference.
units.why: The theorem explains why sampled action scores suffice even though the policy changes future state visits. REINFORCE is the first complete implementation of that result.

next.note: Remove irrelevant rewards and reduce gradient noise.

study.title: CS 185/285 Lecture 5: Policy Gradients
study.locator: Slide 7, REINFORCE, and slides 20 to 23, automatic differentiation and practical implementation

study.title: Sutton and Barto: theorem and REINFORCE
study.locator: Chapter 13, Section 13.2, The Policy Gradient Theorem, and Section 13.3, REINFORCE: Monte Carlo Policy Gradient; printed pp. 324 to 329, including the proof box and REINFORCE algorithm box
study.depth: The authors post the full text free at incompleteideas.net. Use the section titles if your printing has different page labels. Leave the short-corridor training comparison for the baseline unit.

focus: Unroll the Bellman derivative into visitation-weighted action-value terms. The theorem avoids an explicit derivative of the state distribution; it does not assume that distribution is fixed.

For \(J=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}]\), a trajectory-sum estimator uses \(\gamma^t G_t\), where \(G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}r_{k+1}\). Uniform timestep sampling without this outer factor is a different weighting convention.

Use Stable softmax, cross-entropy and loss reductions rather than rebuilding softmax. Minimize the negative weighted log probability, hold return weights fixed, sum within episodes and average over episodes.
units.reproduce: On CPU, enumerate the four trajectories of two independent Bernoulli actions with separate logits initially zero. Let the rewards be \(r_1=a_0\), \(r_2=2a_1\) and \(\gamma=1/2\). Then \(J=p_0+p_1\), so its logit gradient is \((1/4,1/4)\). Implement the negative episode-sum log-probability loss using detached reward-to-go and outer discount weights. Probability-weight its four gradients and get \((-1/4,-1/4)\); check the objective with centered differences in `float64`.
traps: Calling an arbitrary timestep mean the exact episodic gradient. Episode length and the reduction convention affect weighting.
Applying the optimizer before recomputing the batch's action log probabilities, then describing that gradient as on-policy REINFORCE.
Using the policy pseudo-loss as the return metric. Its value is not an estimate of expected return.

selfTest.q: Does the theorem say state visitation is independent of the policy?
selfTest.a: No. It reorganizes the full derivative into an expectation over policy-dependent visits.

selfTest.q: Why is return treated as fixed when differentiating the sampled loss?
selfTest.a: The score-function derivation already accounts for how the policy changes the trajectory law. Differentiating the weight would add a different term.

selfTest.q: In the two-step example, what happens if the outer discount weight is omitted?
selfTest.a: The expected ascent gradient for the second logit becomes \(1/2\), not \(1/4\). The first component remains \(1/4\).

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab REINFORCE with an exact expected-gradient check and fresh-trajectory updates.
units.stopWhen: Your enumerated loss gradients match the objective gradient with the sign reversed, and your derivation states the visitation, discount and reduction conventions.

fit.verdict: The lecture implementation and Chapter 13 proof reach derive and implement depth; policylab supplies the checked update.

units.title: Reward-to-go, baselines, unbiasedness and variance reduction
outcomes: Prove the reward-to-go causality result and conditional baseline unbiasedness.
Distinguish fixed, state-dependent and action-dependent baselines, including a baseline fitted on the same samples.
Measure estimator variance against an exact small-problem expectation.
units.why: A noisy but unbiased gradient and a biased gradient need different repairs. Baselines offer a controlled way to change noise without changing the population target, when their assumptions hold.

next.note: Learn a baseline, then distinguish it from a bootstrapped critic.

study.title: CS 185/285 Lecture 5: variance reduction
study.locator: Slides 16 to 18: gradient noise, Baselines and Causality
study.depth: Slide 17's zero-mean proof applies to a baseline independent of the scored action. Its same-batch mean-return suggestion has finite-sample dependence; test that case separately.

study.title: Causality and the expected score lemma
study.locator: Expected Grad-Log-Prob Lemma, Don't Let the Past Distract You, and Baselines in Policy Gradients
study.depth: Skip the intervening implementation walkthrough; do not install the retired environment stack.

study.title: Sutton and Barto: baseline comparison
study.locator: Chapter 13, Section 13.4, REINFORCE with Baseline, printed pp. 329 to 331; revisit Example 13.1, Short corridor with switched actions, on p. 323
study.depth: The authors post the full text free at incompleteideas.net. Read the comparison as evidence from the book's setup, not a guaranteed learning-speed improvement.

focus: Condition on the history before the action. Earlier rewards are fixed under this conditioning and multiply a zero-mean action score, so they can be removed.
For a fixed baseline, \(\mathbb{E}[b(s)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\mid s]=0\). A state-only input does not ensure independence if fitting used that same action's return.

Variance reduction is not automatic. For a scalar score \(z\), the variance-minimizing constant baseline is \(\mathbb{E}[Rz^2]/\mathbb{E}[z^2]\), when the denominator is positive. It need not equal mean return.
units.reproduce: Reuse the one-step Bernoulli policy with \(p=1/4\) and rewards 2 and -1. Enumerate \(g=(R-b)(a-p)\). All fixed baselines have mean \(9/16\). With \(b=0\), variance is \(75/256\); with the value baseline \(b=-1/4\), it is \(27/64\); with \(b=5/4\), it is zero. Verify these population quantities on CPU by probability-weighting both actions, not by comparing unrelated Monte Carlo runs.
traps: Claiming every value baseline reduces variance. The exact example shows one that increases it.
Subtracting each episode's own return as its baseline. That removes the entire learning signal, not just noise.
Using `detach()` as an independence proof. It blocks an autograd path but does not remove statistical dependence on the sampled action.

selfTest.q: May a baseline depend on the current state?
selfTest.a: Yes, provided it is conditionally independent of the current action. The score has conditional mean zero at that state.

selfTest.q: For independent one-step samples, what happens if every sample subtracts the batch mean return that includes itself?
selfTest.a: With batch size \(N\), the expected sample-mean estimator is \((1-1/N)\nabla J\). The self contribution creates bias; a leave-one-out mean avoids that dependence.

selfTest.q: Why can past rewards be dropped even when past and future rewards are correlated?
selfTest.a: Conditional on the pre-action history, each past reward is fixed and the current score has mean zero. Independence of past and future rewards is unnecessary.

selfTest.q: What should a variance comparison hold fixed?
selfTest.a: The policy, environment, objective, estimator reduction and sampled trajectories. Change only the weighting or baseline, and check expectation against an oracle.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab baseline and reward-to-go comparisons with exact expectations, shared samples and the short-corridor baseline ablation.
units.stopWhen: You prove causality and baseline unbiasedness, reproduce all three exact variances, and explain why same-batch centering needs a separate finite-sample check.

fit.verdict: The lecture, score lemma and Chapter 13 comparison cover the derivations; exact enumeration and the mini-project supply controlled measurement.

units.title: Learned value baselines, critic targets and actor-critic dependencies
outcomes: Explain why a learned Monte Carlo baseline and a bootstrapped actor-critic have different bias sources.
Derive one-step critic targets and actor weights with separate termination and trajectory-boundary semantics.
Implement actor and critic updates with explicit target snapshots and gradient ownership.
units.why: A critic gives credit before an episode ends, but its errors can enter the actor's learning signal. The update order and the target's policy identity are part of the algorithm.

next.note: Combine one-step and longer-horizon actor weights.

study.locator: Slides 4 to 6, 8 to 12, 16 to 17 and 21 to 22: value fitting, bootstrap targets, batch and online actor-critic, critics versus baselines

study.locator: Chapter 13, Section 13.5, Actor-Critic Methods, printed pp. 331 to 332; the One-step Actor-Critic (episodic) box
study.depth: The authors post the full text free at incompleteideas.net. Skip the eligibility-trace algorithm box.

study.title: Homework 2: baseline update dependencies
study.locator: `PGAgent.update`, steps 1 to 4, and `_estimate_advantage`, the baseline branch
study.depth: Read the starter as an update-order audit, not runnable completed code. Its Gym and WandB setup needs porting; implement the update in policylab instead.

focus: Use TD error, TD(0), bootstrapping and Monte Carlo versus TD bias and variance as the earlier result. The new question is how that target weights an action score.

For a snapshot critic, \(y_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma(1-d_t)V_{\text{old}}(s_{t+1})\) and \(\hat A_t=y_t-V_{\text{old}}(s_t)\), where \(d_t\) marks true termination. A truncation needs the final pre-reset observation's value.

Freeze actor weights and critic regression targets for the specified update. Detach the actor's advantage and the bootstrap target; a shared encoder may still receive the separately declared value-loss gradient.
A fixed imperfect baseline subtracted from full returns preserves the score expectation. An imperfect next-state value inside a return target can create action-dependent bias.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write one actor-critic update with separate actor and critic parameters. For reward 1, \(\gamma=0.9\), current value 0.5 and next value 2, get target 2.8 and advantage 2.3. True termination gives target 1 and advantage 0.5; external truncation keeps 2.8 and 2.3 using the final observation. On CPU, backpropagate the actor loss and check that only actor parameters receive gradients; backpropagate the detached-target squared value loss separately.
traps: Refitting the critic and silently recomputing actor weights partway through the same update. That changes the declared estimator.
Treating the baseline network as a critic merely because it is learned. Bootstrapping the action assessment is the relevant distinction here.
Bootstrapping from a reset observation at truncation. That credits the old action with the next episode's value.

selfTest.q: Can a perfect value function make the one-step TD residual an unbiased advantage estimate?
selfTest.a: Yes. Conditional on the state and action, the expected reward plus discounted next-state value equals the action value, so subtracting the state value yields advantage.

selfTest.q: What bias can an imperfect next-state value introduce?
selfTest.a: Its expected bootstrap error can depend on the current action through the transition law. It therefore need not vanish when multiplied by the action score.

selfTest.q: Does detaching the advantage forbid a shared actor-critic encoder?
selfTest.a: No. It prevents the policy-loss gradient from flowing through the advantage calculation. The encoder can still receive gradients through policy logits and the separate value loss.

fit.verdict: Lecture 6 and Chapter 13 distinguish baseline and critic bias; the starter makes update order concrete and policylab checks gradient ownership.

units.title: n-step advantages, Generalized Advantage Estimation and the gamma-lambda trade-off
outcomes: Derive n-step advantages and GAE as a weighted sum of TD residuals.
Implement the backward recursion with separate bootstrap and trace-continuation masks.
Explain the discount and trace-decay endpoints relative to a stated policy-gradient objective.
units.why: GAE controls how much future sampled reward enters the actor weight. Fixed trajectories expose its indexing and boundary bugs before any learning curve can hide them.

next.note: Use frozen advantages in the PPO surrogate.

study.title: CS 185/285 Lecture 6: longer-horizon advantages
study.locator: Slides 23 to 25: n-step returns, Generalized Advantage Estimation and the policy update

study.title: GAE paper: estimator derivation
study.locator: arXiv:1506.02438v6, Section 2, Preliminaries, and Section 3, Advantage Function Estimation, pp. 2 to 5; Equations 14 to 18
study.depth: Stop before Section 4. The paper starts from an undiscounted objective and introduces discounting as an approximation; do not silently identify its discounted gradient approximation with every discounted-objective convention.

study.title: Homework 2: GAE starter contract
study.locator: `_estimate_advantage`, the `gae_lambda` branch and reverse loop
study.depth: The dummy final value and single `terminals` boundary marker are not enough for externally truncated rollouts. Carry final observations and two masks in your own implementation.

focus: Build on n-step returns, target boundaries and fixed-trajectory update oracles. Subtract the current value from each n-step return, then telescope the TD residual sum.

Use \(\delta_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma(1-d_t)V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\) and \(\hat A_t=\delta_t+\gamma\lambda c_t\hat A_{t+1}\). The bootstrap mask excludes true termination; the continuation mask excludes any episode reset and the end of the available segment.
At \(\lambda=0\), use one TD residual. At \(\lambda=1\), a complete terminal episode telescopes to discounted return minus baseline; a nonterminal segment still contains its final bootstrap value.

Changing \(\gamma\) changes the discounted value target, or biases an undiscounted-gradient approximation. Changing \(\lambda\) changes estimator reliance on the critic, not the underlying discounted value function. Lower variance is a tendency, not a theorem for every trajectory law.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement both an explicit TD-residual sum and a backward recursion on CPU. Use rewards \((1,2,3)\), values \((0.5,1,1.5,0)\), true termination after the third reward, \(\gamma=0.9\) and \(\lambda=0.8\). Residuals are \((1.4,2.35,1.5)\) and advantages are \((3.8696,3.43,1.5)\). With \(\lambda=0\), recover the residuals; with \(\lambda=1\), recover \((4.73,3.7,1.5)\). Require absolute agreement within \(10^{-10}\) in `float64`, then add a truncated segment with a nonzero final value.
traps: Cutting both bootstrap and trace at truncation. Cut the trace across reset, but retain the final observation's bootstrap.
Calling the finite-segment trace-decay endpoint pure Monte Carlo while it still bootstraps an estimated tail.
Flattening time and environment axes before the recursion and letting one environment's residual enter another's advantage.

selfTest.q: Why do the intermediate value terms cancel when trace decay is 1?
selfTest.a: Each discounted next-state value cancels the following residual's discounted current-state value. The initial negative value and any final bootstrap remain.

selfTest.q: Does a correct critic eliminate the usual bootstrapping bias for shorter traces?
selfTest.a: For the stated discounted advantage target, yes in conditional expectation. Discounting relative to an undiscounted objective and finite-sample effects are separate issues.

selfTest.q: Which mask applies when an episode ends because of an external time limit?
selfTest.a: Keep the bootstrap from the true final observation, but set trace continuation to zero so the next reset episode contributes nothing.

selfTest.q: At a nonterminal rollout cut, should the value of the next observation be zero?
selfTest.a: No. Use its critic value for the last residual; only the unavailable future residual sum is cut.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab GAE endpoint, termination, truncation and vector-lane oracles, followed by a matched trace-decay ablation.
units.stopWhen: Both GAE implementations match the fixed cases and a nonterminal cut, and changing a reward in one vector lane cannot change another lane's advantages.

fit.verdict: Lecture 6 and the original paper cover n-step and GAE derivations; the starter and policylab boundary oracles supply implementation depth.

units.title: Categorical, Gaussian and tanh-squashed policies and entropy regularization
outcomes: Implement categorical and diagonal Gaussian policy log probabilities with correct event reductions.
Derive the tanh-squashed density and explain why clipping samples is not the same distribution.
Add entropy regularization with the correct loss sign and distinguish base Gaussian from transformed entropy.
units.why: The action passed to the environment and the action whose density enters the update must have a declared relationship. A wrong density can leave training apparently functional while the gradient and PPO ratios are wrong.

next.note: Compare old and new densities of the same action.

study.title: Sutton and Barto: stochastic policy parameterizations
study.locator: Chapter 13, Section 13.1, Policy Approximation and its Advantages, printed pp. 322 to 324, and Section 13.7, Policy Parameterization for Continuous Actions, pp. 335 to 336
study.depth: The authors post the full text free at incompleteideas.net. Focus on policy parameterization; the underlying distributions and transformations are already covered in Common distribution families and transformations.

study.title: PPO continuous-action distribution audit
study.locator: 9 details for continuous action domains: state-independent log standard deviation, independent action components, and Handling of action clipping to valid range and storage
study.depth: Stop before Normalization of Observation. The checklist uses latent Gaussian samples followed by clipping, not a tanh-transformed density.

study.title: The tanh change-of-variables correction
study.locator: arXiv:1801.01290v2, Appendix C, Enforcing Action Bounds, Equations 20 and 21

study.title: PPO entropy term
study.locator: arXiv:1707.06347v2, Section 5, Algorithm, Equation 9 and its entropy-bonus explanation
study.depth: Read only the combined objective here; the PPO surrogate comes next.

focus: Reuse the stable log-softmax and loss-gradient results. A categorical policy produces one log probability per sampled action; independent Gaussian components require a sum across action coordinates, not across the batch.
For \(a=\tanh u\), \(\log\pi(a\mid s)=\log\mu(u\mid s)-\sum_i\log(1-\tanh^2 u_i)\). An additional affine scaling of action bounds adds its log-Jacobian correction too.
Retain the pre-squash action for stable likelihood evaluation near saturation. Clipping is noninvertible and creates boundary masses; do not apply the tanh Jacobian to it.

Minimizing a loss with \(-c_H H\), for positive \(c_H\), encourages entropy. Transformed entropy is \(H(a)=H(u)+\mathbb{E}[\log|\det(da/du)|]\), not merely the Gaussian's analytic entropy. Entropy alone does not guarantee useful state coverage.
units.reproduce: On CPU with `float64`, derive the scalar Gaussian log-density derivatives at fixed action \(u=0.5\), mean 0 and standard deviation 1: the mean derivative is 0.5 and the log-standard-deviation derivative is -0.75. Squashing gives \(a=\tanh(0.5)\approx0.462117\) and corrected log density about -0.803710. Implement the correction and match `torch.distributions.TransformedDistribution` with `torch.distributions.TanhTransform(cache_size=1)` to absolute tolerance \(10^{-10}\).
traps: Keeping a reparameterized sample's gradient path while applying a score-function loss. Hold the sampled action fixed when differentiating its log density.
Evaluating a Gaussian density at the clipped environment action while claiming it is the latent-action score. Store the actual latent sample if using that formulation.
Assuming larger Gaussian standard deviation always means larger bounded-action entropy. Saturation can concentrate transformed actions near the bounds.

selfTest.q: Why sum diagonal Gaussian component log probabilities?
selfTest.a: Their joint density is the product of component densities. Taking its log turns the product into a sum and gives one scalar per action vector.

selfTest.q: Can a continuous action density exceed 1?
selfTest.a: Yes. A density is not a point probability; its integral over the action support must be 1.

selfTest.q: Can the tanh correction cancel in a PPO ratio?
selfTest.a: Yes, for the same action and the same parameter-independent invertible transform under both policies. It still matters for absolute log densities and transformed entropy.

selfTest.q: Which entropy sign encourages exploration in a minimized loss?
selfTest.a: Subtract a positive coefficient times entropy. Adding it would encourage lower entropy.

units.title: Old and new log probabilities, importance ratios and the PPO clipped surrogate
outcomes: Compute new-over-old action-density ratios from frozen rollout log probabilities.
Derive the PPO clipped surrogate and its active gradient branch for each advantage sign.
Implement a minimized clipped loss and verify it on fixed actions before training.
units.why: PPO changes the policy-gradient objective so one rollout batch can support several updates. Its clipping is sign-dependent and must be tested as an objective, not treated as a safety guarantee.

next.note: Measure the drift clipping does not constrain.

study.locator: Lecture 9, Off-Policy Policy Gradient, slides 7 to 10 and 13 to 16: importance sampling, the first-order approximation and clipped weights
study.depth: Distinguish the lecture's approximations from the precise clipped surrogate in the paper. Do not infer exact state-distribution correction from an action ratio.

study.title: PPO clipped surrogate
study.locator: arXiv:1707.06347v2, Section 3, Clipped Surrogate Objective, Equations 6 and 7 and Figure 1, p. 3

study.title: PPO: both advantage signs
study.locator: Key Equations: PPO-Clip, Advantage is positive, Advantage is negative, and the KL early-stopping caveat

focus: Recompute the new policy's log density at the stored observation and stored action. Keep the old density from the behavior-policy snapshot: \(\rho_t=\exp(\log\pi_{\text{new}}(a_t\mid s_t)-\log\pi_{\text{old}}(a_t\mid s_t))\).

Maximize \(\min(\rho_t A_t,\operatorname{clip}(\rho_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_t)\). For positive advantage the upper side saturates; for negative advantage the lower side saturates. Movement in the harmful direction is still penalized.
Minimization requires the negative surrogate, equivalently the maximum of the two negated branches. Old log probabilities and advantages are fixed, while new log probabilities retain their gradient.
The surrogate is a lower bound on the unclipped sampled surrogate, not a general lower bound on true policy return. It does not enforce an actual ratio or KL constraint.
units.reproduce: With \(\epsilon=0.2\), enumerate four samples with \((\rho,A)=(0.6,2),(1.4,2),(0.6,-2),(1.4,-2)\). The maximized per-sample surrogates are \((1.2,2.4,-1.6,-2.8)\); the negative batch mean is 0.2. On CPU in `float64`, differentiate that loss with respect to the four ratios and get \((-0.5,0,0,0.5)\). Check centered differences away from the clipping boundaries.
traps: Putting the old policy on top of the ratio. That reverses the intended correction and clipping cases.
Resampling actions when computing new log probabilities. The ratio must compare densities of the same stored action.
Clamping the ratio and using only that branch. PPO takes a minimum with the unclipped surrogate so harmful changes retain a gradient.

selfTest.q: What ratio should an unchanged policy produce?
selfTest.a: One, up to numerical tolerance, when observation processing, action representation and density evaluation are unchanged.

selfTest.q: Does a ratio above the upper clip boundary always have zero policy-loss gradient?
selfTest.a: No. It is flat for positive advantage, but a negative advantage retains the unclipped harmful-change gradient.

selfTest.q: What happens at zero advantage?
selfTest.a: That sample's policy-surrogate term and its gradient are zero. Value and entropy terms may still update parameters.

selfTest.q: Does the per-action ratio correct the new policy's state visitation distribution?
selfTest.a: No. PPO optimizes a surrogate over old-policy states. Large updates can make this approximation poor.

study.title: PPO diagnostic checklist
study.locator: 13 core implementation details, Debug variables; then 4 auxiliary implementation details, Early Stopping
study.depth: The prose calls clip fraction the fraction triggering clipping. In the code it counts all out-of-interval ratios, including the harmful-direction cases that remain active.

focus: For old-policy actions and common support, \(\mathbb{E}[-\log\rho]=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\text{old}}\|\pi_{\text{new}})\). The control-variate estimate \(\mathbb{E}[\rho-1-\log\rho]\) has the same expectation because \(\mathbb{E}[\rho]=1\). A sampled mean is not the exact KL.
The sample mean of negative log ratio can be negative. The ratio-minus-log expression is nonnegative per sample in exact arithmetic, but neither estimator supplies a hard worst-state bound.
Log ratio quantiles, out-of-interval fraction and the advantage-sign-aware flat-branch fraction separately. Clip fraction alone cannot tell whether the policy loss has saturated.

Several epochs reuse old states, actions and advantages while the learner changes. Freeze the denominator throughout and specify whether the stop signal is minibatch or full-rollout, pre-update or post-update. Early stopping does not undo an update already taken.
units.reproduce: Enumerate a two-action state with old probabilities \((0.5,0.5)\), advantages \((1,-1)\) and \(\epsilon=0.2\). Compare new probabilities \((0.9,0.1)\) and \((0.999,0.001)\). Both have clip fraction 1 and maximized clipped surrogate 0.2, but exact old-to-new KL is about 0.510826 and 2.761231 nats. Probability-weight the two KL estimators and verify agreement with the exact KL within \(10^{-10}\) in `float64`. Then keep the old probabilities frozen while varying the new policy toward a deterministic action.
traps: Refreshing old log probabilities after each minibatch. Ratios then hide cumulative rollout-policy drift.
Reporting a final minibatch's KL as the whole update's KL. Recompute over the frozen rollout if that is the stated diagnostic.
Treating a stop threshold as a constraint. Sampling error, missed states and an already-completed optimizer step can all permit larger changes.

selfTest.q: Which KL direction does averaging negative log ratio over old-policy actions estimate?
selfTest.a: Old-to-new KL, averaged over the chosen old-policy state sample. Swapping the action sampling law changes the interpretation.

selfTest.q: Does a high clip fraction imply most sample gradients are zero?
selfTest.a: No. Only favorable-direction out-of-range cases have a flat clipped policy branch. Harmful-direction cases keep an active gradient.

selfTest.q: Why can parameters still change after many policy-surrogate samples saturate?
selfTest.a: Other samples, shared value or entropy terms, and optimizer state can move them. Saturation of individual terms is not a parameter constraint.

selfTest.q: What happens to old-to-new KL if the new probability of an old-supported action tends to zero?
selfTest.a: It diverges, even when that sample's favorable negative-advantage PPO branch is already flat.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab per-epoch ratio and KL traces, a declared full-rollout stopping rule and a matched update-epoch ablation.
units.stopWhen: You exhibit equal clipped objectives with different KL, distinguish both clip diagnostics, and your epoch trace preserves one behavior-policy denominator.

fit.verdict: Lecture 10, the pinned CleanRL diagnostic code and the checklist cover KL, clipping and repeated epochs; policylab supplies drift measurements.

State the sign, scale and parameter ownership of policy, value and entropy losses.
Test how advantage centering and scaling depend on minibatch composition and standard-deviation convention.
units.why: Two agents with the same PPO surrogate can take different updates because of value clipping, normalization and loss coefficients. These choices need explicit tests and ablations, not a claim that defaults are optimal.

study.title: PPO normalization and value-loss audit
study.locator: 13 core implementation details: Normalization of Advantages, Value Function Loss Clipping, Overall Loss and Entropy Bonus, and Global Gradient Clipping
study.depth: Use Schedules, gradient accumulation and clipping for the earlier global-norm result; focus here on which losses feed that norm.

focus: The rollout return target is frozen, often \(\hat A+V_{\text{old}}\). Normalize actor advantages separately; do not substitute normalized advantages into the critic's target.

Value clipping compares the raw squared error with the squared error at \(V_{\text{old}}+\operatorname{clip}(V_{\text{new}}-V_{\text{old}},-\epsilon_V,\epsilon_V)\), taking the maximum. It is not clipping the target or enforcing a hard bound on value changes.

Centering can change an advantage's sign and therefore its PPO clipping branch. Per-minibatch centering gives a sample different weights in different shuffles; this finite-sample coupling is not evidence of new experience.

Record the normalization scope, standard-deviation correction and small-denominator handling. CleanRL uses `std()` with the default sample correction; singleton minibatches require an explicit policy rather than a silent nonfinite weight.
units.reproduce: On CPU in `float64`, use old value 0, new value 1, return target 2 and value-clip width 0.2. The half-scaled unclipped loss is 0.5; the maximum-based clipped loss is 1.62 and has zero derivative with respect to the new value at this point. Next center advantages \((1,3)\): population-standard-deviation scaling gives \((-1,1)\), while sample-standard-deviation scaling gives \((-1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\). Implement both conventions and keep the critic target unchanged.
traps: Using a minimum for value clipping because the policy surrogate uses a minimum. The pessimistic squared-error loss uses a maximum.
Allowing gradients into old values or return targets. That lets the target move to accommodate the current prediction.
Comparing loss coefficients without recording sum, mean and half-squared-error conventions. Those change the effective gradient scale.

selfTest.q: Why does the reproduced clipped value loss have zero gradient?
selfTest.a: The larger error comes from the clamped value, which is constant in this region. The unclipped branch is smaller and therefore inactive.

selfTest.q: Does centering preserve every sample's PPO clipping branch?
selfTest.a: No. A small positive advantage can become negative after subtracting the batch mean, which reverses the favorable clipping direction.

selfTest.q: Does multiplying advantages by a positive constant change their signs?
selfTest.a: No. It scales the policy-surrogate gradient but not the value or entropy losses. It is not generally equivalent to scaling the whole optimizer's learning rate.

selfTest.q: Should a normalized advantage be used to reconstruct the return target?
selfTest.a: No. Normalization changes the actor weight's units and offset. Use the original advantage plus the frozen old value for that target.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab value-clipping gradients, normalization-scope regressions and a matched value-loss or normalization ablation.
units.stopWhen: Your loss reproduces the flat value-clipping case and both normalization conventions, and changing normalization cannot mutate the frozen return target.

fit.verdict: The paper defines the combined loss, while pinned CleanRL and the checklist supply the missing implementation variants and policylab checks them.

study.title: Control Laboratory: update and identity tests
study.locator: Architecture constraints; Milestone C, Main implementation; Milestone D, Failure handling; Correctness requirements

focus: Extend Trajectory schemas with environment, policy, seed and version identity. Store behavior log probabilities, critic values, observations, actions, rewards, both ending flags, final bootstrap observations and a policy-version identifier.
Keep time and environment axes until GAE is complete. Flatten every field with the same ordering and exclude reset-only entries from policy, critic, entropy and metric reductions.

In Gymnasium 1.4.0 next-step mode, the ending step returns the final observation. The following step ignores that lane's action and returns a reset observation with zero reward and false ending flags; it is not experience from that action.

Separate rollout snapshots from learner state. Re-evaluate stored actions under the unchanged snapshot before the first update; ratios should be 1 within tolerance. Use independent residual sums and finite differences away from clipping kinks as test oracles.
units.reproduce: On CPU with Gymnasium 1.4.0, construct `gym.vector.SyncVectorEnv([lambda: gym.make('CartPole-v1', max_episode_steps=1)])` and call `envs.reset(seed=0)` after assigning it to `envs`. Step with `numpy.array([0])`, then `numpy.array([1])`. The first call has reward 1, `terminated=False` and `truncated=True`; the second has reward 0 and both flags false. Store only the first as a valid transition. Add a second lane with a different time limit and check that masking and GAE remain lane-local.
traps: Storing a reset-only vector step as if its sampled action caused the reset. It creates a fake transition and changes the denominator of loss means.
Recording a policy version without binding observation normalization and action transforms to it. Those can change log probabilities even with unchanged network weights.
Checking only scalar loss equality. Ratio inversion, broadcasting or target detachment defects can require per-sample and gradient tests to expose.

selfTest.q: Why are two ending masks still needed with a valid-transition mask?
selfTest.a: Validity excludes reset-only records. Termination determines whether to bootstrap; episode boundaries determine whether the advantage trace may continue. They answer different questions.

selfTest.q: Can a vector step contain both real transitions and reset-only entries?
selfTest.a: Yes. Lanes end independently, so validity must be tracked per lane, not with one batch-wide flag.

selfTest.q: How do you test that flattening preserves the record?
selfTest.a: Give every time-lane pair a unique label and check that all flattened fields preserve the same label order. Then recover the original axes.

selfTest.q: What must stay fixed during a finite-difference policy-loss check?
selfTest.a: Observations, actions, old log probabilities, advantages and transforms. Perturb only current policy parameters, and avoid nondifferentiable clip boundaries.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab immutable vector rollouts, identity-ratio checks, lane-local GAE and fixed-batch loss and gradient regressions.
units.stopWhen: Your collector excludes reset-only entries, preserves final bootstrap observations and policy identity, and passes independent per-sample, shape and gradient tests.

study.title: Control Laboratory: failure and evaluation evidence
study.locator: Milestone D, Failure handling; Milestone E, Measurement / optimization; Milestone F, Final evaluation; Measurement requirements

focus: Start with invariants: unchanged-policy ratios, reward/action alignment, target detachment and boundary masks. Rising KL, falling entropy or poor value fit are symptoms, not unique diagnoses.

Compare critic predictions with frozen targets using residuals and squared error as well as explained variance. Explained variance can miss a constant prediction offset and is undefined when target variance is zero.

On CPU, use your tested policylab PPO on `CartPole-v1` with Gymnasium 1.4.0. Prespecify five training seeds and 100000 valid environment transitions per seed; record hyperparameters, versions and all attempts. This is an experiment budget, not a return target.

Evaluate frozen checkpoints on separate seed streams, with the action rule declared as sampling or argmax. Plot per-training-seed returns and entropy, KL, value error, ratio and gradient diagnostics against interactions and wall time. Treat the training run, not its many evaluation episodes, as the unit for across-run uncertainty.
units.reproduce: Build two fixed-batch defects on CPU. For old probabilities \((0.5,0.5)\) and new probabilities \((0.8,0.2)\), correct ratios are \((1.6,0.4)\) and exact old-to-new KL is about 0.223144 nats; replacing the denominator with the current policy falsely gives ratios \((1,1)\). Separately, use value targets \((1,3)\) and predictions \((11,13)\): mean squared error is 100 while explained variance is 1. Write regressions that detect both defects without a learning curve.
traps: Calling low entropy policy collapse without checking the task and evaluation policy. A useful deterministic policy can have low entropy; poor independent return and lost action support supply the failure evidence.
Reporting only successful runs or the best checkpoint chosen on final evaluation seeds. Keep failures and separate tuning, checkpoint selection and final evaluation.
Treating training episode returns or a lower pseudo-loss as proof of generalization. Evaluate a frozen policy independently and keep evaluation out of the update data.

selfTest.q: Ratios remain exactly 1 after several optimizer steps. Is that reassuring?
selfTest.a: Not by itself. The actor may not have moved, but the old log probabilities may also have been refreshed incorrectly. Recompute against the immutable behavior snapshot.

selfTest.q: Why can explained variance equal 1 for a poor critic?
selfTest.a: It uses the variance of residuals, which ignores a constant offset. Predictions shifted uniformly from the targets have zero residual variance but nonzero squared error.

selfTest.q: Can many evaluation episodes from one trained model replace multiple training seeds?
selfTest.a: No. They estimate that model's evaluation variability, not variability caused by training randomness.

selfTest.q: What does an entropy-coefficient ablation need for fair attribution?
selfTest.a: The same environment, seed set, interaction budget, evaluation policy and tuning budget, with all attempts retained. Keep unrelated algorithm choices fixed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab multi-seed PPO evidence, independent checkpoint evaluation and two induced ratio, critic or entropy failure postmortems.
units.stopWhen: You detect both fixed-batch defects and retain a complete multi-seed evaluation report with two diagnosed induced failures, raw curves and no best-seed claim.

fit.verdict: The checklist and pinned metric code support diagnosis; the pool's Control Laboratory specifies multi-seed measurement and the mini-project supplies the experiment.
